turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I did the checks on the way in. Blood pressure was one thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-two, oxygen ninety-seven percent. He talked the legs off me about the neighbour's dog.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks a million. In ye come, sit wherever's comfortable. What has ye here today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Sure I'm grand, there was no call for it. The traffic was desperate coming down the town, and yer man in the chemist was giving out yards about the price of the paper.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's not grand, doctor. I'm his wife, I look after him and I do all the tablets. He's repeating questions, he's forgetting appointments, and he got lost last week.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Would you stop. I'm well able. We had a bit of sun yesterday and I had the tea out the back, it was lovely.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): I want to hear the two sides, no hurry. When you say repeating questions, what does that look like at home?
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He'll ask me what day it is three or four times of a morning, and then again after the breakfast. It's been a couple of months now.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not. I'm only making a bit of conversation. Everyone asks the day.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the getting lost. What actually happened?
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Last Thursday he went down for the paper. A neighbour rang me, she'd found him by the church, and he couldn't tell her the way home. It's a walk he does every week.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): I wasn't lost. I took the long way round to see the new houses. I knew rightly where I was the whole time.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the appointments, then.
[SEG0013] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He missed the dentist last Tuesday, and the eye test the Tuesday before that. I had the two of them written on the calendar in the kitchen.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): The eye test, fair enough, I forgot that one. The dentist I did not forget. I wasn't going in that chair, it murders the jaw.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): And the dentist's waiting room smells of that stuff, you know, the clove stuff. I can't be doing with it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Around the house itself, any trouble finding your way about, or finding the words?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Not a bother. Kettle, remote, the good scissors, I know where they all are. I do the crossword most nights.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The house is fine. It's once he goes out the door.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): The Saturday crossword in the Times was a pure terror, mind. I was at it half the day and the radio on for the hurling.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you're out walking, any chest pain, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Chest is grand, wind is grand. The only stress is that dog next door barking at the postman every morning.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who looks after the medicines?
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I do, every bit of it. In the morning he has the ramipril for the blood pressure.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): The little white one. That's ten milligrams, isn't it?
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It is not. The box says five milligrams. One tablet every morning, I put it in his hand and he swallows it.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand, we'll take it as five milligrams. Is there another one in the morning?

[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The water tablet. That's the furosemide, forty milligrams, one every morning, for the swelling in the ankles. Some mornings he refuses it though. Maybe twice in the week he won't take it.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): It has me running to the toilet, and I can't be doing with that if we're going anywhere. So I leave it those days.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you on anything for the cholesterol, a statin?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): The atorvastatin, twenty milligrams. I stopped that. The legs were aching something awful on it.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He stopped it himself back in March. The box is still in the press and he won't go back on it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the aspirin they spoke about at the hospital, did you ever actually start that?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I never took it. I don't like the notion of thinning the blood.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He never started it, that's right.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing. I can take the lot, as far as I know.
[SEG0037] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We've never come across any.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the blood pressure been going on?
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Years. He's been on the ramipril a good five years at least, from the GP in town.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Longer than that, I'd say. It was before the Galway trip, and that was a great week, we walked the prom every evening and the weather held.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the blood pressure is one we already know about. Any operations down the years?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Not a one. They've never had to open me, thank God.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): And at home, it's the two of ye?
[SEG0044] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It is. He's retired off the buses these ten years. I'm in the house with him all day.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Dublin Bus, the number ten. I could call every stop from here to the Phoenix Park. Don't mind her saying I'm away with it.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me just look at the ankles while you're here. They're soft, there's no swelling today, and the pulse is nice and regular.

[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not putting a name on any of this today. I'd like to send you for bloods, full blood count, kidney function, thyroid, and B12 and folate. And I'll arrange a memory assessment.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): A memory assessment? I'm not gone soft in the head. My uncle used to forget his hat in every pub and he could still add a docket in his head.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's only to have a proper look, not a label. And I'd ask you not to go walking off on your own for the moment, until we've a bit more information.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll go with him for the walks. That's no trouble.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): If it's dry I'll still want the long way round. But alright, I hear you.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in to me in a fortnight, the bloods should be through by then, and we'll go over them.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): A fortnight, grand. Will I bring the crossword in to prove a point? I'm only messing.
[SEG0054] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods at the desk on the way out, and I'll put the fortnight into the diary.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect, thanks. Mind yourselves on the way out, and we'll see ye then.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

omissions.text: Furosemide 40 mg every morning is only partially adhered to: some mornings he refuses it, about twice a week, because it makes him run to the toilet, especially if they are going anywhere.
Atorvastatin 20 mg was stopped by the patient himself back in March because his legs were aching badly on it, and he refuses to restart it.
Aspirin had been advised by the hospital but he never started it because he does not like the idea of 'thinning the blood'.
The caregiver reports he is forgetting appointments, specifically he missed the dentist last Tuesday and the eye test the Tuesday before, despite both being written on the kitchen calendar.
No allergies were reported by both patient and caregiver; caregiver confirmed they have never come across any allergies.
No swelling in the ankles today was specifically described as soft edema absent, and the pulse was nice and regular on examination.
He has had hypertension for at least five years on ramipril from the GP in town, possibly longer per patient.
The doctor said he was not putting a name on this today.
The caregiver agreed she would accompany him on walks pending further information.
Nurse planned to book the blood tests at the desk on the way out and enter the fortnight follow-up in the diary.
